content.title: Italian Court Confirms Law Limiting Citizenship Claimed by Descendants Abroad
content.text: An Italian law restricting the granting of citizenship for those born abroad has been approved by the country’s highest court, signaling the end of a longstanding practice that allowed people to obtain a passport on the basis of ancestry alone.Citizenship by bloodlineThe law that was announced by the Meloni government on Mar. 28, 2025 dictates that people seeking to apply on the basis of being the descendent of an Italian citizen – a legal principle known as jus sanguinis – can do so only if they have an Italian citizen parent or grandparent. Prior to the change, the only limit on the rule was that the Italian ancestor had to have been alive when the Kingdom of Italy was founded in 1861, a structure that allowed people to obtain citizenship through a great-great grandparent, or even farther back, if they could document it.Other aspects of the law set limits for those with dual citizenship by dictating that they must “engage” by paying taxes, voting, and renewing passports and other IDs or risk losing their Italian citizenship.Not a “novelty”At the time of the law’s passage, Italian Foreign Minister Alberto Tajani stated that the measure was meant to crack down on people who seek the passport as a “novelty” or for the sole purpose of getting around travel restrictions. Italy’s passport is one of the most welcomed in international travel, tied for fourth place in the Henley Passport Index with eleven other European Union member states for being accepted in 185 countries worldwide.Tajani’s office says that the number of Italian citizens living abroad grew from 4.6 million to 6.4 million between 2014 and 2024, mostly from Argentina and Brazil – two countries with some of the largest populations from the Italian diaspora. They note a sharp rise in applications for citizenship, with Argentina’s Italian consulate processing 30,000 applications in 2024 alone, a 50 percent rise from the previous year. Brazil processed 20,000 applications in 2024, and grew by a similar margin over the previous year.Tajani said when the citizenship law was passed last year that it was meant to rectify “abuses and requests for citizenship that went a bit beyond the true interest in our country.”The caseFour judges in Italy tried to appeal the new standard to the country’s Constitutional Court, which issued a statement after a hearing for one of the cases on Wednesday calling the appeal “partially unfounded and partially inadmissible.” The statement is broadly viewed as rendering the three remaining challenges moot. A more detailed verdict is expected sometime in the next few weeks.In the case brought before Italy’s highest court, government lawyers successfully argued that Italians’ descendants abroad were not actually citizens at birth, but that they were born with the expectation of citizenship, and that claiming it past the date set in 2025, then they had a “fictitious link” to the country and forfeited their right to it.Corrado Caruso, a professor at Bologna University who argued the case against the law at the court, told CNN the fact that consulates “couldn’t keep up” with the requests likely played a part in the change, along with the fact that many who obtain citizenship do not move to Italy or pay taxes there. He also believes that the move might have been motivated by international politics: “These citizens could move around the world on their Italian passports, so maybe there was some pressure from Italy’s historical allies.”“A right nobody can touch”Others, like citizenship lawyer Marco Mellone, are already preparing to appeal to the last legal authority beyond the Constitutional Court, the Court of Cassation. While the Foreign Ministry points to practical concerns and issues of social cohesion, Mellone sees a fundamental legal principle at stake that dates back to Italy’s 1861 unification. “Descendants were born Italian citizens. If you are a citizen at birth, you have a right that nobody can touch,” he told CNN. “You can’t say, what I said when you were born was not true, you’re not an Italian citizen anymore. You can’t say, I was joking.”
